newsitem.title: LEBANON: FOCUS-Lebanon sells bank to Saudi billionaire.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Lebanon sells bank to Saudi billionaire.

text.p: Lebanon's central bank announced on Thursday the sale of its 97 percent stake in medium-size Credit Libanais bank to billionaire Saudi Sheikh Khalid bin Mahfouz for $163 million.

Credit Libanais, acquired by the Bank of Lebanon in 1989 as the result of a financial crash, is a commercial and investment bank with an extensive credit card business and a 3.43 percent market share.
Its 45 branches comprise Lebanon's biggest retail banking network.
CL's assets at end 1996 totalled $898 million -- 10th in the sector. Shareholders' equity was eighth at $66 million at profits ranked 24th at $3.55 million.
Central bank Governor Riad Salameh said in a statement that the Bank of Lebanon had decided to sell its share in Credit Libanais to two companies headed by Sheikh Khalid bin Mahfouz.
Capital Investments Holding - Bahrain would take 65 percent of the bank's shares and Capital Investments Holding - Lebanon would take the other 32 percent, the statement said.
"As a result of this operation the Bank (of Lebanon) will acquire liquidity of about $163 million," it said.
The billionaire Sheikh Khalid bin Mahfouz took over Saudi Arabia's biggest bank, National Commercial Bank (NCB), in July 1996. He is general manager and chairman of the bank.

Governor Salameh told Reuters the central bank received several bids for Credit Libanais, mainly from Arab and Lebanese investors. It announced in May that it had decided to sell its stake by private placement.
Salameh said Sheikh Khalid bin Mahfouz made the highest bid and was also considered a strategic investor because the sale would bring the Saudi and Lebanese banking sectors closer together.
"We believe strategically at the central bank that opening up of the financial markets to many sectors in the area is profitable to Lebanon," Salameh said in a telephone interview.
"This (sale) is going to be a very efficient tool for bringing together the banking and financial markets in Saudi Arabia and Lebanon," he added.

Asked whether Lebanese banks would be unhappy about the decision, Salameh said: "I think, anyway, it is in the interest of the banking sector because an investor of this magnitude means we have a good banking sector with good prospects."

Sheikh Khalid bin Mahfouz would continue to develop Credit Libanais and would maintain its present banking products and staff, Salameh said. According to the almanac of the Lebanese Banks Association, CL has 750 employees.
"There were no conditions attached to the sale but it is understood that it will be that way," Salameh said.
